title: How Flatterers Should Be Avoided
coreMove: Design counsel so truth is invited from chosen people, heard patiently, and closed by the prince's own steady decision.
sourcePressure: The chapter warns that courts are full of flatterers, but letting everyone tell the truth lowers respect. The third course is to choose wise men, let them speak truth only when asked and only on the matters asked, question them broadly, listen patiently, decide personally, and remain steadfast. Maximilian shows the opposite: secretive, pliant, obstructed, changing daily, and therefore contemptible.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The wrong version says leaders should listen to feedback. The writer must preserve the design problem: uncontrolled truth lowers majesty, closed secrecy produces bad execution, and wisdom lies in controlled invitation plus final authority.

counterintuition: most people assume more advice is better, but actually less is better
tryThisNow: set a timer for ninety seconds and ask for feedback

exampleSpecs.domain: a war council where every noble tries to advise the prince in the corridor before the formal question is asked
exampleSpecs.audience: a prince protecting truth from flattery without making every hallway a council chamber
exampleSpecs.stakes: if anyone can advise at any time, respect falls and advice becomes pressure; if no one can answer, snares go unseen
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The prince closes the corridor petitions box, unlocks the small council tablets, and asks the three named captains the river-crossing question in order.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A corridor petitions box sits locked beside three small council tablets.

exampleSpecs.domain: a mint reform delayed because the ruler reveals his plan only after dies have already been cast
exampleSpecs.audience: a secretive ruler learning why late disclosure invites obstruction and reversal
exampleSpecs.stakes: moneyers object after the design is public, and the ruler keeps changing symbols until nobody trusts tomorrow's coin
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The auditor lays three canceled coin dies in a row and marks where the ruler should have asked the assay master before casting the first one.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Three canceled coin dies sit beside an unopened assay note.

exampleSpecs.domain: a plague quarantine board where physicians flatter the prince by saying every district is healthy
exampleSpecs.audience: a prince choosing which advisers may speak hard truths without general license for panic
exampleSpecs.stakes: comforting reports keep court calm while infection crosses districts; uncontrolled rumor would also destroy order
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: He sends the smiling health summaries back, names two physicians and one burial clerk to answer only the fever-map questions, then waits through the answer without interrupting.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Smiling health summaries cover the edge of a fever map.

exampleSpecs.domain: a dam reservoir court where engineers, millers, and priests all press different counsel before spring thaw
exampleSpecs.audience: a ruler who must question broadly but decide singly
exampleSpecs.stakes: divided advice can either reveal the whole risk or make the ruler pliant and contemptible if he changes with each speaker
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: After hearing each group separately and together, the ruler puts one spillway marker on the reservoir board and refuses to move it when the last delegation returns.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A wooden spillway marker sits on a reservoir board wet with thaw maps.

exampleSpecs.domain: a frontier embassy where courtiers praise a dangerous treaty because they think the prince wants it
exampleSpecs.audience: a prince testing whether advisers tell truth or mirror appetite
exampleSpecs.stakes: a court trained to please will mistake his first leaning for command and leave the frontier exposed
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The prince places his own draft face down, asks for objections first, and notes which councillor still praises the hidden clause he has not shown.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A face-down treaty draft lies beside a tray of blank objection slips.

exampleSpecs.domain: a canal lock emergency where the prince asks too late and then accepts every new opinion in sequence
exampleSpecs.audience: a secretary documenting how flattery and pliancy turn one decision into several undone decisions
exampleSpecs.stakes: lock crews cannot rely on a ruler whose morning order is reversed by noon and revived by dusk
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The secretary pins the morning red flag, noon white flag, and dusk red flag to the lockhouse wall until the crews see why no one moved.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Red and white order flags hang together on a lockhouse wall.

skillTargets: distinguish controlled invitation of truth from open advice that lowers respect
apply the sequence ask broadly, listen patiently, decide personally, remain steadfast
analyze flattery as mirroring appetite rather than telling useful truth
evaluate whether a ruler's counsel system creates wisdom or produces Maximilian-style secrecy and reversal

tryThisNowSpec: Choose one decision a ruler must make. Name the three people allowed to speak truth, the exact question each may answer, and the point at which advice closes and decision begins.
